question: Can an activation that weights inputs by their value, xPhi(x), the expectation of an input-dependent stochastic mask, beat ReLU and ELU across vision, NLP and speech tasks?
hypothesis: A nonlinearity that is the expectation of a stochastic regularizer (input-dependent Bernoulli(Phi(x)) mask) will match or exceed ReLU and ELU.
contributions: Introduce the GELU, xPhi(x), as the expectation of a modified Adaptive Dropout mask
Empirical comparison against ReLU and ELU on MNIST, TIMIT, Twitter POS and CIFAR-10/100
Coin the SiLU, x*sigma(x), and give tanh and sigmoid approximations of the GELU

method.summary: Replace the activation in existing architectures with GELU (mu=0, sigma=1, tanh approximation) and compare with ReLU and ELU(alpha=1) on six tasks, tuning only the learning rate over {1e-3,1e-4,1e-5} and reporting medians over 3-5 runs.
method.task: activation function comparison (classification, autoencoding, tagging, frame recognition)

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.split: 5k validation examples held out from train for learning-rate tuning

datasets.name: Tweet POS (Gimpel 2011; Owoputi 2013)
datasets.preprocessing: pretrained word vectors from 56 million tweets; input is concatenation of target word and left/right neighbour vectors

datasets.name: TIMIT
datasets.preprocessing: 11 frames input, 26 MFCC, energy and derivative features per frame; 39 phone labels

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.split: 5k validation for lr tuning, then retrain on whole train set
datasets.preprocessing: ZCA whitening, Gaussian noise sigma=0.15, no data augmentation

models.name: Tweet tagger
models.architecture: two-layer network, 256 neurons per layer, dropout keep probability 0.8

models.name: TIMIT classifier
models.architecture: five-layer, 2048 neurons wide, dropout rate 0.5 (Mohamed et al. 2012)

models.name: CIFAR-10 CNN
models.architecture: 9-layer conv net from Salimans & Kingma 2016 with batch norm (Table 1: 3x3 convs 96/192 channels, 1x1 convs, dropout p=0.5, global avg pool)

models.name: WideResNet 40-4 (CIFAR-100)
models.architecture: wide residual network, 40 layers, widening factor 4, Conv-Act-Conv-Act-BatchNorm block

training.objective: log loss for classification; mean squared error for autoencoder
training.optimizer: Adam (MNIST, autoencoder, Twitter, TIMIT, CIFAR-10); Nesterov momentum with SGDR schedule (CIFAR-100)
training.lr: tuned over {1e-3,1e-4,1e-5} on validation; autoencoder 1e-3 and 1e-4 (0.01 tried: ELU diverged)
training.lr_schedule: CIFAR-10: linear decay to zero from epoch 100 of 200; CIFAR-100: SGDR T0=50, eta=0.1
training.epochs: 50 (MNIST), 250 shown in Fig 4 (autoencoder, read from Fig 4), 200 (CIFAR-10), 50 (CIFAR-100), 30 shown (TIMIT, read from Fig 5)
training.dropout: MNIST none and 0.5 keep; Twitter keep 0.8; TIMIT 0.5; CIFAR-10 p=0.5; CIFAR-100 keep 0.7
training.regularisation: dropout; Gaussian input noise 0.15 on CIFAR-10
training.seeds: median of 5 runs (MNIST, Twitter, TIMIT), 3 (autoencoder, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100)

other.GELU: mu=0, sigma=1, no new hyperparameters; tanh approximation used in every experiment

inference.samples: median of 3 or 5 runs per setting

metrics.name: test error
metrics.definition: classification error rate (median over runs, chosen at lowest validation error for TIMIT)

eval.protocol: Median over 3 or 5 runs; no significance tests; learning rate tuned per nonlinearity on validation data.

evidence.quote: we use the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015) rather than stochastic gradient descent without momentum

results.claim: GELU gets lower CIFAR-10 median error than ReLU and ELU.
results.setup: 9-layer CNN, CIFAR-10, no augmentation, Adam 200 epochs, median of 3 runs
results.quote: Ultimately, the GELU obtains a median error rate of 7.89%, the ReLU obtains 8.16%, and the ELU obtains 8.41%.

results.claim: GELU on CIFAR-100 WideResNet 40-4 beats ReLU and ELU.
results.setup: WRN 40-4, 50 epochs, SGDR, Nesterov, keep 0.7, median of 3 runs
results.quote: the GELU achieves a median error of 20.74%, the ReLU obtains 21.77%

results.claim: Original 40-4 WideResNet with ReLU obtains 22.89% (reported from Zagoruyko & Komodakis).
results.quote: the original 40-4 WideResNet with a ReLU obtains 22.89% (Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2016)

results.claim: ELU on CIFAR-100 WRN median error.
GELU Twitter POS median test error is lowest.
results.setup: two-layer net, 256 units, 5 runs per learning rate, median
results.quote: the median test set error is 12.57% for the GELU, 12.67% for the ReLU, and 12.91% for the ELU

results.claim: GELU TIMIT frame classification median test error is lowest.
results.setup: 5-layer 2048 net, 5 runs, test error at lowest validation error
results.quote: median test error chosen at the lowest validation error is 29.3% for the GELU, 29.5% for the ReLU, and 29.6% for the ELU

results.claim: SiLU performs worse than GELU but usually better than ReLU and ELU.
results.quote: we found that a Sigmoid Linear Unit (SiLU) xσ(x) performs worse than GELUs but usually better than ReLUs and ELUs

results.claim: GELU approximation used in all experiments.
results.quote: we used the former in every experiment in this paper

limits: Medians over only 3-5 runs, no variance or significance tests; gaps are 0.1-1 point.
Only small models and datasets (MNIST, TIMIT, tweets, CIFAR); no transformer or language-model experiments.
Only ReLU and ELU compared; SiLU claim has no numbers; learning rate is the only tuned hyperparameter.
Autoencoder, MNIST and robustness results are shown only as figures.
Appendix B gives the authors' account of priority disputes over SiLU/swish; it is their own account.

lineage.note: GELU is the expectation of a modification of adaptive dropout, with a Gaussian not logistic CDF
MNIST experiment replicated from this paper

figures.caption: The GELU (mu = 0, sigma = 1), ReLU, and ELU (alpha = 1).
figures.why: shows GELU as a smooth non-monotonic ReLU

code.snippet: GELU(x) = x Phi(x) = x * 1/2 [1 + erf(x/sqrt(2))]; approx 0.5x(1 + tanh[sqrt(2/pi)(x + 0.044715x^3)]) or x sigma(1.702x)
